title: Why Phonics and Fish Don't Exist
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos uses the "constrained vs. unconstrained skills" distinction from reading researcher Scott Paris to argue that phonics instruction is being systematically overtaught relative to what the evidence supports. Drawing on David Share's self-teaching hypothesis, Wiley Blevins's list of common phonics-instruction failure modes, and an SRI Education finding that 58% of observed K-2 classrooms never had students read text longer than individual words, she contends that phonics should function as a transitional means to the end of automatic word recognition, not an end pursued indefinitely. Borrowing the central conceit of Lulu Miller's Why Fish Don't Exist, Janetos argues "phonics" is, like "fish," a convenient but artificially bounded label rather than a coherent, self-contained skill -- useful precisely because it has no fixed boundaries, but also prone to expanding past its usefulness into activities like affricate terminology drills that the research does not support. Her conclusion is not anti-phonics but pro-"planned obsolescence": teach the code efficiently, then move deliberately into using that code to read, build vocabulary, and write.
points: Janetos's central argument, built on Scott Paris's constrained/unconstrained skills framework, is that phonics is a finite, transitional skill that should be taught efficiently and then deliberately retired in favor of connected reading -- not indefinitely reinforced.

An SRI Education learning brief found that in 58% of observed K-2 classrooms, students never read text longer than individual words, evidence she cites that phonics instruction is crowding out application to actual connected reading.

Citing David Share's self-teaching hypothesis, she argues that once students have cracked the alphabetic code, further exposure to real text -- not more isolated phonics drilling -- is what builds orthographic mapping and vocabulary.

Her extended metaphor, borrowed from Lulu Miller's Why Fish Don't Exist, holds that "phonics," like "fish," is a useful but artificial category with no natural boundary, which is exactly why it is prone to overextension into instruction the research does not support, such as teaching kindergartners technical terms like "affricates."
quotes: This essay proposes that some reading skills, such as learning the letters of the alphabet, are constrained to small sets of knowledge that are mastered in relatively brief periods of development. In contrast, other skills, such as vocabulary, are unconstrained by the knowledge to be acquired or the duration of learning.
This strikes me as a massive overstretch of what the research actually supports, and I can't see it makes any sense to be spending 10 lessons teaching it to all kindergarten kids.
In 58% of the K-2 classrooms, students did not read text longer than individual words.

Many of the issues in education arise because we judge the 'doing' as the destination. We can't become so fascinated by the mechanism for doing decoding that we forget the meaningful application of our instruction to accessing books.

The term fish turns out not to be a coherent biological category. It's a label for a collection of creatures that don't all share a unique common ancestry. So there is no evolutionary branch that contains all fish and only fish - hence, its location in limbo.

We don't abandon phonics because we think it's failed; we abandon it because it's outlived its usefulness and generates opportunity costs since it was never intended to dominate the literacy landscape and can too easily block the access road to real reading.
